rows.text: Racial inequality discourse in academia is overwhelmingly shaped by a combination of disciplinary gatekeeping, standpoint epistemology, cumulative scholarly momentum, team-level epistemic diversity, and broader socio-political climate, which together explain why social_science ranks first with the strongest positive association: papers published in social-science journals (sociology, political science, psychology, ethnic studies) are structurally oriented toward power, identity, and stratification topics, whereas natural sciences, engineering, and technology fields rarely engage these specific racial keywords. This disciplinary primacy is followed by black (second, positive) because standpoint theory and historical patterns of scholarly mobilization predict that author teams with higher estimated shares of Black scholars are far more likely to foreground lived-experience-driven questions of racial bias, discrimination, and justice. Third, paper_inequality_mentions_3_years (positive) captures path-dependent academic momentum: once inequality scholarship gains traction in the preceding three years, citation networks, special issues, and funding incentives pull subsequent papers into the same conversation. Authors_race_diversity_score ranks fourth (positive) under the assumption that racially mixed teams—measured via Shannon entropy on inferred country-of-origin racial probabilities—introduce complementary perspectives that surface racial inequality where homogeneous (often White-dominated) teams might overlook or deprioritize it. Finally, news_inequality_mentions_3_years (positive) reflects the external feedback loop from media and social movements (e.g., post-2014 BLM spikes) that primes academic agendas, even though the measure aggregates all inequality forms; together these five features dominate because they operationalize the core mechanisms of institutional, identity-based, temporal, collaborative, and societal drivers while other variables (gender share, field diversity scores) operate more indirectly or conditionally.

I ranked "black" first because the share of Black authors is the most direct proxy for whether a paper discusses racial inequality -- researchers from underrepresented groups are more likely to study topics related to their own experiences. "social_science" is ranked second because racial inequality is predominantly studied within social science disciplines (sociology, political science, economics), making it a strong domain-level predictor. "authors_race_diversity_score" ranks third: more racially diverse author teams bring broader perspectives and are more likely to engage with inequality topics. The two time-lagged features ("news_inequality_mentions_3_years" and "paper_inequality_mentions_3_years") capture the zeitgeist effect -- when inequality receives more attention in media and academia, researchers across fields are more likely to address racial inequality in their work. All signs are positive because higher values of each feature should increase the probability that a paper discusses racial inequality.

For (1.) social_science, (2.) natural_science and (3.) engineering_and_technology, I apply the same logic as the case of gender inequality. I think that the scores of (4.) news_inequality_mentions_3_years and (5.) paper_inequality_mentions_3_years are good indicators as well, since people tend to choose topics that are popular in media and academia.

I expect disciplinary location (social_science) to be the most important predictor because racial inequality is fundamentally a social, political, and historical phenomenon that is theorized and empirically studied primarily within the social sciences. Journals in sociology, political science, social psychology, history, and related fields are institutionally oriented toward structural inequality, discrimination, and justice, making explicit racial inequality language far more likely. Second, I rank paper_inequality_mentions_3_years highly because academic research agendas are path-dependent and shaped by intellectual trends; when inequality discourse rises within academia, scholars are more likely to frame their work using inequality-related concepts and keywords. Third, news_inequality_mentions_3_years captures agenda-setting effects from broader society: heightened media attention to racial justice or hate crimes can increase funding, scholarly motivation, and perceived relevance, thereby raising the probability of racial inequality mentions. Fourth, I predict a positive effect of the Black author share, based on standpoint theory and representation mechanisms—scholars from historically marginalized racial groups may be more attuned to race-related questions or more motivated to study racial inequality. Finally, I include authors’ racial diversity score because more racially diverse teams may bring broader perspectives and lived experiences, increasing the salience of race as an analytic dimension. Overall, my ranking assumes that structural disciplinary incentives and temporal discourse trends exert the strongest influence, followed by compositional effects of research teams.

I rank social_science first because papers in social science fields are the most likely to study inequality as a central social phenomenon and to use explicit language such as discrimination, bias, justice, and stereotypes in titles or abstracts; by contrast, many papers in other fields may address related problems without naming them in inequality terms. I place paper_inequality_mentions_3_years second because scholarly discourse is path dependent: when inequality becomes more salient in the recent academic literature, authors are more likely to frame their own contributions using that vocabulary, so I expect a strong positive diffusion effect. I rank black third because a higher estimated share of Black authors may be associated with greater attention to racial inequality through standpoint, topic selection, professional networks, and sensitivity to race-related harms, which should raise the likelihood of explicit mention. I place news_inequality_mentions_3_years fourth because academic research is also shaped by the broader public agenda; when inequality is more visible in the news, scholars may respond by studying those issues or by describing their work in more publicly legible inequality language. Finally, I rank authors_race_diversity_score fifth because racially diverse teams may bring a wider range of experiences and perspectives, making them somewhat more likely to identify racial inequality as theoretically and empirically important. Overall, my signs are positive because each of these features should, through disciplinary orientation, discourse diffusion, or team composition, increase the probability that a paper explicitly mentions racial inequality.

I rank social_science as the most important feature because racial inequality is primarily conceptualized, measured, and debated in fields such as sociology, political science, psychology, economics, history, and related social-science disciplines; therefore, a paper published in a social-science journal should be much more likely to contain keywords such as racial discrimination, racial bias, racial justice, or racial stereotypes. I rank paper_inequality_mentions_3_years second because academic discourse is path-dependent: when inequality becomes more visible in recent scholarly publications, authors are more likely to frame new work using similar concepts and terminology, producing a positive association. I rank news_inequality_mentions_3_years third because public discourse can shape academic agendas, especially for topics such as racial violence, hate crime, racial justice, and discrimination; however, I expect this effect to be somewhat weaker than prior academic discourse because scholarly publishing responds with delays and is filtered through disciplinary norms. I rank black fourth because I assume that papers with a higher estimated share of Black authors may be more likely to study or foreground racial inequality, either because of lived experience, research specialization, or stronger sensitivity to racialized institutions, though this effect is likely smaller than field-level and discourse-level effects. Finally, I rank authors_race_diversity_score fifth with a positive sign because racially diverse author teams may bring a wider range of perspectives and research questions, increasing the likelihood that racial inequality becomes salient in the title or abstract; however, this is ranked lower because team diversity is an indirect predictor and may partly overlap with author racial-composition measures. These judgments rely on the feature definitions in the attached document, including the discipline indicators, lagged inequality-discourse measures, inferred author racial composition, and racial-diversity entropy score.

My reasoning is anchored in a layered model of scholarly production, where a paper's topic is first and foremost shaped by the epistemological boundaries of its discipline, and then further modulated by the social positionality of its authors. At the foundational level, a discipline defines what constitutes a legitimate object of inquiry. Social science disciplines, such as sociology and political science, are built around the systematic study of social structures, power, and inequality; racial inequality is therefore not a peripheral concern but a central and theoretically prized subject. This makes social_science the most powerful positive predictor. The categorical opposite is equally informative: a paper in the natural_sciences is, by institutional and epistemological design, oriented toward biophysical processes rather than social ones, creating a powerful negative constraint on the likelihood of engaging with racial inequality discourse. This disciplinary context sets the broadest possible stage on which other factors operate. Operating within this stage, I draw on standpoint theory and the sociology of knowledge to argue that lived experience shapes scholarly attention. The share of black authors is my second-most important predictor because scholars from communities directly subordinated by racial hierarchy possess a distinctive "insider" perspective-a combination of personal motivation to understand and dismantle that hierarchy and privileged epistemic access to its nuances. This resounds as a strong positive signal, particularly given the anti-Black focus historically embedded in many racial inequality keywords. Extending this logic of positionality from the individual to the collaborative team, the authors_race_diversity_score captures a positive, dynamic effect. A racially heterogeneous team does not simply pool static identities; it creates a micro-social environment where contrasting perspectives must be negotiated, often sparking explicit inquiry into the very nature of racial difference and inequality that the team enacts. Finally, while the Black experience is a central axis of racial discourse, other marginalized groups also experience racialization; thus, a greater share of hispanic_and_other authors similarly predicts a higher likelihood of engaging the topic, though with a comparatively less consistent signal than the Black share given the keyword list's specific thematic gravity.

If this paper is about social science, it's more likely to discuss the race inequality issue. So I think the subject of the paper is the most important thing. Therefore, I ranked the subject variables as the top feature. Then, I assume that black researchers will be more interested in this topic, so I ranked black as the second most important feature. The total number of paper about inequality in the last 3 years may also have a positive correlation with our prediction, as it captures the trends of discussing any form of inequality in academia. If the number of authors is large, it is more likely this is a natural science paper and thus less likely that it talks about race inequality.If there is female author in the paper, it's also more likely that the authors are into inequality topics.

The domain which the paper belongs to is the most important indicator, in my opinion. A social science paper is more likely to talk about racial inequality rather than natural science or engineering and technology papers. If academic papers mention inequality in the past 3 years, that could be an indicator that the topic is getting attention in academia. And inequality being mentioned in the news for the past 3 years is a less strong indicator that academics could be interested in conducting research in this topic.

I believe two components are important: 1) a general trend of research, and 2) the identity of the authors. So I think the trend in academic publications and the country's racial inequality background are the most important, followed by their own races and racial composition of the author team. Social science is important as I assume inequality is rarely discussed outside of social science.

In the social sciences, researchers almost always collect participants’ demographic information: age, gender, race, education, and socioeconomic status. This reflects the notion that demographics matter for understanding the human condition. In the social sciences we study: stratification, hierarchy, schooling, policing, discrimination, inequality, labor markets, and related topics, variables that are both theoretically relevant and relatively easy to collect and analyze are more likely to appear in published papers.

I also think that women tend to research, and be involved in, research on social issues because, compared to other fields, it is often seen as less prestigious or high status, and it can create a less aggressive culture that feels more inclusive and welcoming.

Overall, I think there are more white researchers, so we see their over-representation in any field. But as race-related research becomes more central, I also think we will see more whites in that area as well.

Moreover, I believe that news and papers can have a lasting impact on discourse, on people’s memory, and on what feels urgent or important in the current zeitgeist, and therefore will affect the amount and direction of subsequent research.

Social science is again the primary field in which racial diversity is studied. 
In my experience, black and minority race individuals are much more likely to focus on conducting research on topics of racial inequality. While individuals, on the other hand, is much less likely to do that given the lack of knowledge on the issue. 
Country race diversity score is an important factor as racial inequality is much less of an issue in countries that lack diversity to begin with, e.g. China.

Similar to gender, I expect that the relevance of these topics will be more pronounced in the social sciences (where it is an established topic of study) and will follow the tendencies of me-search (i.e., issues of racial inequality will be more personally relevant to black academics) and the flow of trends

I believe that a paper on racial inequality will most likely be published in the field of social sciences. I also believe it is more likely to come from countries where this is a popular topic of discussion, particularly countries with high racial diversity. Additionally, I think that authors publishing on this topic are more likely to be from ethnic minority groups in the countries where they live, typically Black or Latino scholars, especially in the United States.

If a paper is published in a social science journal, compared to other journals from other domains, it has a higher probability of being about racial inequality. So, journal domain is one of the most determinative effects compared to other four factors. 

If inequality is a current theme that the population is concerned about, and this can be due to any population-level issue (e.g., Black Lives Matter), we would expect an increase in media coverage of inequality. This increase in public concern leads to a growing public need for explanation and solutions, thus, academic attention would shift toward inequality research. High coverage of inequality in news may directly increase the probability of a current paper focusing on racial inequality, as editors are more likely to be influenced by public issues. 

Also, high coverage of inequality in news would increase the number of papers focusing on inequality within the last three years, and this would further increase the probability of a current paper focusing on one component of that general issue, namely racial inequality.

Lastly, even though we cannot draw complete causal chains between author demographics and a domain they prefer to investigate (e.g., there might be other factors explaining this link such as early socialization), a team of researchers who has a higher representation of female and black authors might have a higher probability of publishing in a social science journal, which potentially increases the probability of their paper being about racial inequality.  This is not a direct causal link, but, being a member of an underprivileged or disadvantaged category would increase their intention to investigate social issues, or be more perceptive towards those, and shape their academic interests in a way that it would align more with social science journals.

This topic of racial inequality is usually more considered in social science. The black people tend to experience racial inequality more, so a paper with many black authors may be an indicator of this topic. Since this topic of research is inherently diverse, a paper with high diversity score imply that racial inequality is one potential good fit in terms of research topic. Author list with lower country_race_diversity_score may imply that most of the authors are from countries that are not diverse in races (like some European countries) and thus more likely exhibit racial inequality. Finally, many papers discussing inequality in the past 3 years mean that the topic of inequality subsuming racial inequality is trendy now.

I expect social_science to be the most important positive predictor because racial inequality is most often theorized, measured, and explicitly named in fields such as sociology, political science, psychology, history, and related disciplines, whereas other fields are less likely to use that language directly in titles or abstracts. I rank paper_inequality_mentions_3_years second, with a positive sign, because research agendas tend to diffuse over time: when inequality becomes more prominent in recent academic discourse, later papers are more likely to adopt similar concepts, keywords, and framing. I place black third and assign it a positive sign because I assume that author positionality matters: teams with a higher estimated share of Black scholars may be more likely, on average, to study racial stratification, discrimination, and justice, either through lived experience, intellectual commitment, or network ties to those literatures. I rank authors_race_diversity_score fourth, also positive, because more racially diverse teams may bring a wider range of perspectives and problem definitions, increasing the likelihood that racial inequality becomes visible as a research topic. Finally, I assign white a negative sign and rank it fifth because, at the aggregate level, teams with a higher share of White authors may be somewhat less likely to center racial inequality explicitly, reflecting differences in social position, research priorities, or disciplinary subfield sorting. Overall, my ranking assumes that both disciplinary location and author social composition shape what problems are seen as important enough to name directly, while broader academic trend effects influence whether such topics are framed in inequality-related terms.

Social science is more likely to do research on racial inequality (as opposed to STEM or medicine, where gender is a basic characteristic used in analysis). White might be less likely because they are less affected by racial inequality and while they recognize it might not pursue it as a research topic. The diversity of the author group and country racial composition could similarly encourage research in racial inequality. Racial inequality is more politically charged, so news inequality mentions in the last 3 years could be predictive.

first is social_science, which I think will be most predictive as it's the field most focused on these issues, similar to gender inequality. Then, I rank Black as strongly positive, just building on representation theory (again, like gender inequality) where scholars from marginalized racial groups may be more likely to prioritize research questions around racial inequality. my third predictor is author_race_score which I think will capture the idea that racially diverse teams likely will bring heightened sensitivity or focus to these questions. Fourth, I expect white to be negatively associated partly because of assumptions about what topics white researchers prioritize (or deprioritize) but also because of the greater representation of the racial group in the academy. fifth, i thought paper_inequ_mentions would be another positive predictor (although the weakest) because rising academic attention to racial inequality could have similar diffusion effects to the gender context and lead to an epistemological shift

My ranking reflects a simple causal hierarchy in which disciplinary context dominates, discourse environment amplifies, and author standpoint selects. Discipline comes first because the corpus spans fields with radically different objects of study, and racial inequality is constitutively a social-science problem—the concepts, methods, and journals that even permit such keywords are concentrated in sociology, political science, and psychology—so social_science is the strongest positive signal and engineering_and_technology its mirror image: these fields' epistemic agenda (systems, formalisms, devices) almost never engages racialized social relations, making it a powerful negative predictor. (I rank engineering above natural_science as the negative because it is the largest "never-discusses-race" bloc in a corpus heavy with CS, math, and engineering.) Next I place the two lagged discourse measures, invoking an agenda-setting / issue-attention logic: scholarship is responsive to the salience of inequality in the surrounding intellectual and public sphere, so when academic and news attention to inequality has been high in the prior three years (e.g., the post-Ferguson/BLM period), the supply of and receptivity to racial-inequality papers rises—both positive. I rank paper_inequality_mentions above news because academic publishing responds more directly and with shorter lag to its own field's attention cycles than to general news, though the two are correlated. Finally, black author share enters as a positive but lower-ranked predictor via a standpoint and topic-selection mechanism: scholars who have lived experience of, or community proximity to, racial disadvantage are disproportionately likely to choose it as an object of study. I rank it last and modest in magnitude for two reasons—the name-and-country-based inference is noisy and the base rate of Black authors in the corpus is low, both of which attenuate the observable association—so while theoretically central, its predictive contribution should be smaller than the structural discipline and discourse signals above it.

Racial inequality is fundamentally a social phenomenon, so the disciplinary location of a paper should be the strongest predictor: social science fields (sociology, political science, psychology, history) possess the conceptual vocabularies, theoretical traditions, and normative concerns that make racial inequality a legitimate and recurring object of study, which is why social_science ranks first with a positive sign and natural_science ranks fourth with a negative sign—natural science journals rarely engage racial categories as analytic constructs and their scope structurally crowds out such discussion. The composition of the author team matters next, reflecting a "standpoint" or lived-experience mechanism: scholars from groups that historically experience racial marginalization are disproportionately likely to research it, both because personal salience shapes research agendas and because of selection into fields and topics, so black is ranked second with a positive sign. Third, paper_inequality_mentions_3_years captures the discursive opportunity structure of academia—when inequality is already a prominent theme in the recent scholarly conversation, individual authors are more likely to frame their work in those terms due to citation incentives, agenda contagion, and the legitimation of the topic, yielding a positive association. Finally, authors_race_diversity_score is ranked fifth and positive on the assumption that racially heterogeneous teams bring varied perspectives and heightened sensitivity to racial dynamics, increasing the probability that race-related questions surface in the work, though I rank it lowest because team diversity is a weaker and more indirect signal than an author's own background or the field's disciplinary norms.

The selection and ranking of features for predicting mentions of racial inequality in academic papers are grounded in both theoretical and empirical reasoning about how scholarly discourse is shaped by disciplinary norms, author demographics, and broader socio-political contexts. At the top of the ranking, social_science is identified as the most important feature due to the inherent focus of social science disciplines on studying societal structures, power dynamics, and inequalities. Fields like sociology, political science, and psychology explicitly examine racial inequality as a core area of inquiry, making it highly likely that papers from these disciplines will engage with the topic. This assumption aligns with decades of research showing that academic disciplines are not neutral but are shaped by their epistemological and methodological commitments, which often prioritize certain topics over others.

The second and third ranks are occupied by black and authors_race_diversity_score, respectively. These features reflect the role of author identity and team composition in shaping research agendas. The rationale here draws on theories of standpoint epistemology, which argue that individuals' social positions-such as race-shape their perspectives and the issues they prioritize in research. Authors from racial minority groups, particularly Black scholars, may be more likely to study racial inequality due to lived experiences, academic interests, or a commitment to addressing systemic disparities. Similarly, diverse author teams are more likely to bring a range of perspectives to their work, increasing the likelihood that racial inequality will be addressed. This is supported by research on team diversity, which suggests that heterogeneous groups tend to explore a broader array of topics and are more innovative in their approaches.

The fourth-ranked feature, news_inequality_mentions_3_years, captures the influence of the broader socio-political environment on academic research. Scholars do not operate in isolation; their work is often responsive to public discourse, policy debates, and societal events. When racial inequality is prominently discussed in the media-such as during periods of social unrest or policy reforms-academics are more likely to engage with these issues in their research. This reflects the "issue-attention cycle" in public policy and media studies, where heightened public awareness of an issue leads to increased academic focus.

Finally, hispanic_and_other is ranked fifth, as it shares a similar theoretical basis with the black feature. Authors from Hispanic and other racial minority backgrounds may also prioritize research on racial inequality, though the effect may be slightly less pronounced compared to Black authors due to differences in the historical and contemporary salience of racial justice movements. The positive sign for all these features assumes that greater representation of marginalized groups and higher diversity in author teams correlate with a higher likelihood of addressing racial inequality, reflecting both the intrinsic motivations of scholars and the structural opportunities afforded by diverse collaborations.

In summary, these rankings and signs are based on the interplay of disciplinary focus, author identity, team diversity, and the broader socio-political context-all of which shape the likelihood that racial inequality will be a central topic in academic papers.

I ranked social_science as the most important positive predictor because racial inequality is primarily conceptualized, measured, and debated in fields that study social hierarchy, institutions, discrimination, identity, and public policy. Papers in sociology, political science, psychology, economics, history, and related areas are therefore much more likely to explicitly use terms such as racial discrimination, racial bias, racial diversity, or racial justice. I ranked the estimated share of Black authors second, with a positive sign, because scholars from racially minoritized groups, especially Black scholars in the U.S. context, may be more likely to study racial inequality due to lived experience, intellectual traditions, community relevance, and professional networks centered on race and inequality. I ranked paper_inequality_mentions_3_years third because academic discourse is cumulative: when inequality becomes more visible in recent scholarly work, new papers are more likely to adopt similar concepts, keywords, and framing. I ranked news_inequality_mentions_3_years fourth because public attention to inequality can shape research agendas, funding priorities, and the perceived urgency of studying race, although I expect this media effect to be somewhat less direct than prior academic discourse. Finally, I assigned white a negative sign because author teams with a higher estimated share of White authors may, on average, be less likely to foreground racial inequality than teams with more racially minoritized authors. This does not imply individual-level intent; rather, it reflects an expected aggregate association between social position, scholarly specialization, and topic selection.

The theoretical importance and ranking of these features are grounded in the principles of standpoint epistemology and sociocultural agenda-setting. The "Black" identifier is ranked as the primary predictor based on the assumption that a researcher’s lived experience and social identity—often referred to as positionality—are the strongest drivers of their research agenda; scholars from marginalized groups are theoretically the most likely to dedicate their intellectual labor to investigating the structures of their own marginalization. This is followed by the "News Inequality Score," which reflects the cultural zeitgeist. The reasoning here is that academic inquiry does not happen in a vacuum; a heightened public and media focus on inequality creates a feedback loop of institutional funding and social urgency that nudges researchers toward these topics.

The "Social Science" designation is ranked third, serving as the necessary methodological container; while identity and environment provide the "why," this discipline provides the specific qualitative and quantitative tools required to analyze race as a social construct. The "Author Race Diversity Score" and "Country Race Diversity Score" follow as secondary environmental factors. The assumption is that diverse collaborative teams and heterogeneous national contexts increase the "salience" of race, making it a more frequent subject of academic scrutiny through constant exposure to cross-cultural frictions. I anticipate a positive sign for all five features: as the researcher’s identity aligns with the subject, the media environment emphasizes inequality, and the disciplinary and demographic contexts become more diverse, the statistical probability of the paper focusing on race inequality increases. This reflects a belief that research is a direct byproduct of the scholar's identity filtered through their socio-political and institutional environment.

I chose these interactions because I expect the effect of broader discourse and author identity to depend strongly on disciplinary context. The interaction between social_science and paper_inequality_mentions_3_years should be positive because academic attention to inequality is most likely to diffuse into new papers within fields that already treat inequality as a central theoretical and empirical object. In other words, when inequality becomes more common in recent academic discourse, social-science authors are especially likely to adopt those concepts, keywords, and problem framings in their own titles and abstracts. The interaction between social_science and black should also be positive because the relationship between Black authorship and racial-inequality mentions is likely strongest in fields where race, discrimination, racial justice, and institutional inequality are legitimate research topics; in more technical or natural-science fields, author standpoint may have less opportunity to shape the explicit framing of the paper. Finally, the interaction between social_science and news_inequality_mentions_3_years should be positive because public attention to inequality is more likely to influence disciplines that study social problems, institutions, politics, and collective behavior. Overall, these interactions assume that macro-level discourse and researcher standpoint do not operate uniformly across academia, but are amplified when disciplinary norms provide concepts, methods, and publication venues for discussing racial inequality.

The selection and ranking of second-order interactions for predicting mentions of racial inequality in academic papers are grounded in theories of social identity, disciplinary norms, and the broader socio-political context that shapes scholarly work. The social_science × black interaction is considered the most important because it combines two of the strongest individual drivers of research focus: the disciplinary emphasis on social issues and the lived experiences or academic priorities of Black authors. Social science fields, by their nature, are designed to interrogate power structures, inequality, and marginalization, making them fertile ground for discussions of racial inequality. When Black scholars—who may have personal or professional stakes in racial justice—are part of these disciplines, the likelihood of addressing racial inequality is further amplified. This interaction reflects the idea that identity and disciplinary culture are not additive but multiplicative; the presence of Black authors in social science contexts creates a synergistic effect, as their perspectives and priorities align with the field's focus on societal inequities.

The social_science × authors_race_diversity_score interaction is ranked second because it captures how diversity within a discipline already attuned to social issues can deepen and broaden the exploration of racial inequality. Diverse author teams bring varied experiences and viewpoints, which can enrich theoretical and empirical approaches to studying inequality. In social science disciplines, where methodological pluralism and critical perspectives are valued, diversity is not just a demographic feature but a catalyst for more nuanced and inclusive research agendas. This interaction assumes that diversity is most impactful when embedded within a disciplinary culture that actively encourages the study of inequality, thereby reinforcing the importance of both context and composition in shaping research outcomes.

Finally, the news_inequality_mentions_3_years × black interaction is ranked third, reflecting the dynamic relationship between public discourse and academic research. When racial inequality is prominently discussed in the media, it signals a heightened societal awareness and urgency, which can motivate scholars—particularly those from marginalized groups—to engage with these issues in their work. For Black authors, whose experiences and academic interests may already be attuned to racial justice, a surge in public attention to inequality can provide both validation and impetus to contribute to the conversation. This interaction underscores the idea that research is not conducted in a vacuum; it is responsive to the socio-political environment, and the alignment of author identity with public discourse can create a powerful impetus for scholarly engagement with racial inequality. Together, these interactions highlight how disciplinary norms, author identity, and external context intersect to shape the content and focus of academic research.

While news mentions and paper mentions of racial inequality can both serve as the source of researcher's perceived importance of this issue, I think if both news and paper mentions of racial inequality in previous years are higher, it suggests that both the academia and the public are interested in and care about this issue. Therefore, I would think that this will add additional incentive to researchers' study of the topic, thus the production of relevant papers. For the other two interactions, my considerations are mainly based on observations that the racial inequality discussion is mainly focused on black and hispanic groups. If the black or hispanic authors demonstrate higher share, while the authors are likely to come from countries with high racial diversity, I think the author list will care more about the issue of racial inequality, so the probability to produce relevant papers should be further higher.

It's difficult to know! I think that the growing salience of race issues will be most strongly experienced in areas that are primed to recognize them. That includes countries where diversity increases the salience of racial issues, and fields (social science) where they are more relevant. Even as race takes on a growing importance in society, it will remain of less interest to other fields and in countries where it is seen as less relevant.
I also suspect that within more diverse countries it is black academics who are more drawn to these questions.

The first two categories are the same as for the gender version, as (social science, news mentions) determines the popularity and how timely the research is within the research community; and (news mentions, paper mentions), though a bit repetitive with the first one but I still believe will be picked up by the ML model, jointly determines the popularity of the racial-equity research within the society. Finally, (social science, black) jointly determines the relevance of the research for the scholar themselves, where the relevance is in terms of both relevance to the field and the relevance to their own social groups.

Social_science x black is likely positive since racial inequality research is concentrated in social sciences, and Black authors may increase the likelihood that racial issues are explicitly addressed. They reinforce attention to racial inequality. For black x paper_inequality_mentions_3_years, it should be positive Black authorship may further increase the probability that inequality is framed in racial terms after seeing peer academic papers on similar issues. For social_science x paper_inequality_mentions_3_years, it's also likely positive, as inequality-focused trends within social science disciplines are especially likely to sustain and deepen discussion of racial inequality over time.

All three interactions share one underlying logic: disciplinary membership is the gatekeeping condition that allows other forces to express themselves as racial-inequality discourse. I treat `social_science` not merely as an additive booster but as a moderating context — an enabling ecology with the vocabulary, theoretical traditions, journals, reviewers, and reward structures that make naming racial inequality both legitimate and publishable. Outside that ecology (e.g., in engineering or the natural sciences), the same impulses have no sanctioned outlet, so their slopes flatten toward zero. This is why every interaction I selected is positive and why each pairs `social_science` with a force whose effect I believe is latent until a field activates it. For the first and most important interaction, `social_science × paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` (+), my assumption is that the temporal "salience wave" of inequality attention does not lift all fields equally: when ambient scholarly attention to inequality rises (e.g., after 2013 and especially 2020), social scientists are positioned to ride that wave — reframing projects, launching new ones, and citing the moment — whereas a chemistry or mechanical-engineering paper is largely insulated from it, so the wave's predictive power is concentrated where the mandate exists. The third interaction, `social_science × news_inequality_mentions_3_years` (+), is the same mechanism operating one step upstream through the public sphere: media-driven salience translates into academic framing chiefly among scholars whose discipline treats public social problems as legitimate objects, so media climate matters far more for social-science output than for technical fields. The second interaction, `social_science × black` (+), reflects a standpoint-times-opportunity logic: a scholar's social position may generate motivation and lived urgency to study racial inequality, but motivation converts into a published, keyword-bearing paper only where the field affords the topic — so the standpoint effect of Black author share is amplified inside social science and muted where the discipline offers no path to publish such work. The governing assumption across all three is multiplicative gating rather than simple addition: temporal climate, public attention, and authorial standpoint are best understood as potentials whose realization is conditional on a permissive disciplinary environment, which is why the interaction terms carry real, positive explanatory weight beyond the main effects.
I think a social science journal reaches a large audience, and as the number of papers and news articles increases, their combined effect can therefore predict race.
